analytic.title: Global schedulability analysis of a synchronization protocol based on replenishment-bounded overrun for compositional real-time systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Hierarchical scheduling frameworks (HSFs) provide means for composing complex real-time systems from welldefined independently developed and analyzed subsystems. To support shared logical resources requiring mutual exclusive access in two-level HSFs, overrun without payback has been proposed as a mechanism to prevent budget depletion during resource access arbitrated by the stack resource policy (SRP). The same mechanism can be applied to support scheduling techniques, such as fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS), that aim at a reduction of the architecturerelated pre-emption costs and may improve the feasibility of a system. Whereas the blocking times and overrun budgets for shared logical resources will typically be much smaller than the normal budget, these values may significantly increase for scheduling techniques such as FPDS. In this paper, we therefor consider replenishment-bounded overrun, i.e. the overrun ends upon a replenishment, because the normal budget becomes available again, which allows for larger overrun budgets. We show that the global schedulability analysis for this special kind of overrun has a number of anomalies: (i) the usual theorem for critical instant does not hold, (ii) maximal blocking does not necessarily lead to a maximal response time, and (iii) it is not sufficient to analyse a fixed amount of time (say, a number of hyperperiods). We present analysis for two subsystems 1 .

div.head: A. Background
div.p: Hierarchical scheduling frameworks (HSFs) have been introduced to support hierarchical processor sharing among applications under different scheduling services [1]. An HSF can be represented as a tree of nodes, where each node represents an application with its own scheduler for scheduling internal workloads (e.g. tasks) and resources are allocated from a parent node to its children nodes. The HSF provides means for decomposing a complex system into well-defined parts called subsystems. It essentially provides a mechanism for timing-predictable composition of coarse-grained subsystems. These subsystems can be independently developed, analyzed and tested. Temporal isolation between subsystems is provided through budgets which are allocated to subsystems.

Looking at existing industrial real-time systems, fixedpriority scheduling (FPS) is the de facto standard of task scheduling, hence we focus on an HSF with support for FPS within a subsystem. Having such support will simplify migration to and integration of existing legacy applications into the HSF. Our current research efforts are directed towards the conception and realization of a two-level HSF that is based on (i) FPS for both global scheduling of budgets allocated to subsystems and local scheduling of tasks within a subsystem, (ii) the periodic resource model [1] for budgets, and (iii) the Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [2] for both local and global resource sharing.

Subsystems may share global logical resources requiring mutually exclusive access. An HSF without corresponding synchronization support is not realistic, since tasks in subsystems may for example use operating system services, memory mapped devices and shared communication devices. If a task that accesses a global shared resource is suspended during its execution due to the exhaustion of the corresponding budget, excessive blocking periods can occur which may hamper the timeliness of other subsystems [3]. The overrun without payback mechanism [4], [5] can be used to prevent depletion of a budget during global resource access by temporarily increasing the budget with a statically determined amount for the duration of that access. The term without payback means that the additional amount of budget does not have to be paid back during the next budget period. To distinguish this additional amount of budget from a normal budget, we will use the term overrun budget. In the remainder of this paper, we call this form of scheduling HS-o, for hierarchical scheduling with overrun. Improvements of the original schedulability analysis for HS-o can be found in [6], [7].

div.head: B. Motivation
div.p: The global schedulability analysis in [4] is based on the assumption that the overrun budget is smaller than the normal budget. Moreover, it is stated that for well-constrained applications, the global resource access time will typically be much smaller than the normal budget. In this paper, we allow the overrun budget to become substantial compared to (or even larger than) the normal budget. This is motivated by the observation that arbitrary preemptions of tasks and subsystems may cause significant runtime overhead and high fluctuations in execution times, in particular due to architecture-related preemption costs [8], such as cache misses and pipeline flushes. Scheduling techniques aiming at a reduction of these preemption costs, such as fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS) [9], may therefore significantly increase blocking times and overrun budgets. Moreover, limitedpreemptive scheduling techniques have the additional advantage that they may improve the feasibility of a system [10]. As embedded systems are to a great extent resource constrained, limited-preemptive scheduling techniques, such as FPDS, are therefore particularly attractive for embedded real-time systems.

In this paper, we consider a special kind of overrun, termed replenishment-bounded overrun, which allows for larger overrun budgets [11], [12]. This kind of overrun is based on the observation that the overrun budget is merely meant to prevent budget depletion during global resource access. The key idea behind this kind of overrun was to let overrun end upon replenishment of the normal budget, that is, the part of the overrun that falls past the moment of replenishment is charged to the normal budget of the next budget period. Alternatively, one can interpret this form of scheduling as having a form of limited payback: only the overrun that falls in the next budget period is paid back during the next budget period. In the remainder of this paper, we call this form of scheduling HS-rbo, for hierarchical scheduling with replenishment-bounded overrun. The implementation of HS-rbo has been described and compared with other forms of hierarchical scheduling with global resource sharing in [13].

div.head: C. Goal
div.p: HS-rbo was conjectured to have better schedulability [11], [12], but, to the best of our knowledge, no schedulability analysis for it yet exists. In this paper, we make the first steps towards such an analysis, perhaps in a rather unorthodox way.

div.head: D. Approach
div.p: We model HS-rbo schedulability by describing a deadline miss of a subsystem as a set of constraints on the start and end times of jobs. This set of formulae has a number of free variables, such that if there are instantiations for these variables, then it is possible for a subsystem to miss a deadline when the system is scheduled by HS-rbo. Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) gives us a framework that can find instantiations for these free variables (see e.g. [14], [15] for an overview). This approach allows us to do some observations that influence the design of a schedulability test for HS-rbo.

div.head: E. Contributions
div.p: We have investigated a form of scheduling that is likely to perform better than HS-o. Although no full schedulability analysis is presented, we do present results that indicate that an HS-rbo schedulability test cannot be a simple extension of the HS-o test. In particular, we show the following:

• Simultaneous release with all higher priority subsystems is not a critical instant for a subsystem. • Maximal blocking does not necessarily lead to a maximal response time. • Deadlines may be missed after an amount of time that is arbitrarily much larger than the hyperperiod of the subsystems. Furthermore, we present an analysis for the restriction of the problem to two subsystems.

div.head: F. Overview
div.p: The rest of the paper is organised as follows. The next section describes the exact setting we are working in. Section III fixes some terminology that may not be considered standard by all readers. In section IV, we explain how SMT can be used to encode the schedulability problem. Then sections IV-B and IV-C give constraints that are specific to HS-rbo; first the constraints are given for a 2-subsystem setting, then they are extended to deal with more subsystems. Section V then elaborates on some of the results that we obtained using the SMT model. These observations lead us to the analysis for the 2-subsystem case that is presented in section VI. We wrap up with some concluding remarks and suggestions for future work.

div.head: II. PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: We consider the problem of global scheduling analysis of synchronization protocols based on SRP (Stack Resource Policy) and replenishment-bounded overrun without payback for fixed-priority scheduled HSFs.

We assume a set R of globally shared resources, that is used within a system. A system S consists of a list of subsystems S 0 , . . . , S N (for some N ≥ 0). We restrict the problem by assuming that global resource access is non-preemptive, i.e., only one subsystem can access resources at any moment in time, and while a subsystem is accessing resources, it cannot be preempted.

A subsystem S i is characterized by a tuple P i , Q i , X i , where P i , Q i and X i are all real numbers. Q i is the amount of processing time that must be available for a subsystem every P i time units. This periodicity is strict: if a subsystem starts at time t, then Q i time units of processing time must have been available to the system at time t + P i , and another Q i units must be available between t + P i and t + 2P i , etc. (speaking in terms of deadlines: the deadline for the budget of a system is equal to that system's period).

A subsystem consists of tasks (which we will not describe in detail here; we refer the interested reader to [4], [5]), which are scheduled by some local scheduling algorithm to run within the budget of the subsystem. The characteristics of the tasks and the local scheduling algorithm give rise to determine X i , which is the maximum time that any task within the subsystem can access any of the resources in R. If a task is accessing a resource, other tasks that need the resource need to wait until it is released.
We assume that HS-rbo is used for global scheduling, so priorities need to be assigned to subsystems. We do this by assuming that S i has a higher priority than S j if and only if i < j.

For subsystem S i , the global scheduling algorithm reserves processing time every P i time units. The time that must be reserved concretely in the n th period of subsystem S i is called a job and is denoted i, n . It can be characterized by a starting time, an end time and in some cases intervals in which it is waiting for other jobs.

The first period of any subsystem can start at any time; in other words, we assume arbitrary phasing of subsystems. Given the above assumptions, we try to answer the question whether HS-rbo is able to schedule a system such that every job i, n is assigned at least Q i processing time within the corresponding period.

div.head: III. TERMINOLOGY
div.p: To avoid confusion, we dedicate a separate section to fixing the terminology that we will use throughout the remainder of this paper.

We already stated that we assume arbitrary phasing of subsystems. Concretely, this means that the first budget period of every subsystem may start at an arbitrary point in time. We call the start of a budget period the arrival time of a job. Arbitrary phasing then amounts to saying that the arrival times of the first job of every subsystem are chosen arbitrarily.

The start time of a job is the moment in time that a job first consumes processing time. The finalisation time of a job is the first moment from which no more processing time is reserved for that job. We use the term engagement time to refer to the right-open interval between start and finalisation time.

If a job's start time is later than its arrival time, then we say that it was deferred. In some cases we need to be more specific, and we will say the job was delayed if it was deferred because a higher priority subsystem was running when the job arrived. If it was deferred due to a lower priority subsystem that was holding a shared resource, thus preventing the job from being scheduled directly, then we say that the job was blocked.

Furthermore, job i, n preempts job j, m if and only if the start time of i, n occurs while j, m was running. In particular, if in this case a third job preempts i, n , then this third job does not preempt j, m .
Given this definition of preemption, we define the waiting time of a job to be the sum of the engagement times of the jobs that preempt it.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY AS A SATISFIABILITY PROBLEM
div.p: A system is schedulable if and only if there is no possible execution that witnesses its unschedulability, i.e., if and only if no execution exists in which a subsystem does not get the required processing time in one of its budget periods. Rather than trying to directly establish which systems are schedulable, we try to characterise such executions.

We do so by treating the start times and finalisation times of jobs as variables that are subject to a number of constraints that follow from the system specification and the fact that jobs are scheduled using FPPS. By adding extra constraints that say that at least one instance of one subsystem must miss its deadline, we have specified a witness for the unschedulability of a system. We will henceforth call such a witness a failure trace.

Once unsatisfiability is stated as a set of constraints on these variables, we can try to automatically find instantiations for these variables using a technique called satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). Further information about SMT solving can be found in [14], [15], and the Z3 and Yices tools that implement SMT solving are discussed in [16], [17], respectively. If a SMT solver can find an assignment to the variables such that all constraints are satisfied, then the system corresponding to the set of constraints is not schedulable. Moreover, the values assigned to the variables can be retrieved from the SMT solver and used to reconstruct an execution in which a job misses its deadline.

Our reasons for choosing SMT as a formalism are purely practical. In many real-world applications, SMT proves to be an efficient way to solve relatively large problems. Our aim is to develop a closed expression that characterizes schedulability, so using first-order logic seems a natural choice. The theory of real numbers allows us to use a dense time domain. There are a number of different SMT solvers, the interface of which is standardised by the SMT-LIB format, and tool output is easy to parse. As a result, we found it was quite straightforward to implement our ideas in SMT and to visualise the results.

div.head: A. Model
div.p: For each job i, n , we have the following variables. The arrival time of the job is stored in the variable a n i . Likewise, we define variables s n i for the start time and f n i for the finalisation time.

We introduce redundant variables for some other quantities, to ease our job of specifying constraints. The engagement time e n i abbreviates f n is n i . The waiting time is calculated as the sum of all engagement times of jobs that preempt it (here collected in the set W n i ):
div.formula: W n i = { j, m | j = i ∧ s n i < s m j < f n i ∧ s m j < a n+1 i } w n i = j,m ∈W n i e m j -w m j .
div.p: The fact that HS-rbo discards overrun time upon replenishment has an unfortunate side effect; a resource that is acquired in one job might be released in the next job (because the overrun of a job is interpreted as computation time of the next job). We choose to formulate the behaviour differently to make modelling easier: if overrun extends into the budget period of the next job for some amount of time, then budget of the next job is decreased by that amount. For the assignment of computation time to tasks, this reinterpretation makes no difference; the only effect is that the overrun of a job is counted as computation time for that job, instead of as computation time for the next job. This causes the budget Q i of subsystem S i to vary per job. We will use q n i to denote the actual budget for a job i, n . It is defined as follows:
div.formula: q 0 i = Q i q n+1 i = Q i -max(f n i -a n+1 i , 0)
div.p: The overrun time v n i can now be defined as an abbreviation for e n i -w n i -q n i . The use of these variable names is illustrated by Figure 1.
div.formula: S 0 a l 0 s l 0 f l 0 S 1 a m 1 s m 1 f m 1 S 2 f n-1 2 a n 2 s n 2 f n 2 w n 2 w n 2 + q n 2 v n 2 e n2
div.p: Fig. 1. A part of a timeline for three subsystems, annotated with some of the SMT variables that encode the scenario.

div.head: B. Constraints for 2 subsystems
div.p: The following list presents the constraints on these values for each job i, n for a 2-subsystem setting. In the next section we will extend this model to be able to deal with N processes. Each constraint should therefore be read as being quantified over by a universal quantifier over jobs i, n . We leave out this quantification for readability.
1) Jobs do not start before they arrive.
div.formula: a n i ≤ s n i
div.p: 2) A job is only deferred if it arrived when a lower priority job was running that was able to defer it, or if a higher priority job was running or arrived simultaneously.
div.formula: (s n i > a n i ) ⇒ ∃ j,m ((s m j < a n i < f m j ∧ i < j ∧ s n i -a n i < X j ) ∨ (s m j ≤ a n i < f m j ∧ i > j))
div.p: It is here that we rely on the assumption that there are only two subsystems: when there are more, a whole sequence of higher priority jobs might be preventing the job from starting.
3) The engagement time of a job is at least the computation time for the subsystem plus the time it was preempted by other jobs. It is less than the maximum resource access time longer than that.

q n i + w n i ≤ e n i < q n i + w n i + X i 4) If j, m starts between the arrival time and finalisation time of job i, n , then subsystem S j has a higher priority than subsystem S i and j, m ends before i, n does.
div.formula: ∀ j,m a n i ≤ s m j < f n i ⇒ (j < i ∧ f m j < f n i )
div.p: 5) When a job can be scheduled, it will be scheduled. That is to say, jobs are scheduled by a non-idling scheduler. We effectively encode this by stating that if a job is finalised between the arrival time and finalisation time of another job, then that job was preempting another job. This excludes scenarios in which a job is deferred, but does not start immediately when processing time is available.
div.formula: (∃ j,m a m j ≤ f n i < f m j ) ⇒ (∃ j,m s m j ≤ f n i < f m j )
div.p: 6) A job cannot end in the overrun time of another job (in that case, the other job has already had its budget, and that subsystem would not be allowed to run again until its next replenishment).
div.formula: ¬(∃ j,m f m j -v m j ≤ f n i < f m j )
div.p: The question we put to the SMT solver is whether enough time is reserved for a subsystem within one period, given the above assumptions. In terms of variables, this corresponds to satisfying the following formula:
div.formula: ∃ i,n f n i -a n i -v n i > P i
div.p: To solve this set of constraints, we used the SMT solvers yices (see [17], version used was 1.0.31) and Z3 (see [16], version used was 2.19). Because these solvers do not yet deal well with quantifiers, we generated SMT formulae in which the quantifiers are instantiated for a limited number of jobs for each subsystem. This limits the accuracy of the model (a deadline miss will not be detected if it occurs after a sufficiently large amount of time), but it is sufficient to provide us with some interesting insights.

The SMT solvers provide us with mappings from variable names to values that satisfy the given conditions. It is important to notice that these values are nothing more than a witness for satisfiability, and that the particular witness that is given depends on the implementation of the solver. The graphical depictions of failure traces (like the one in Figure 4) in the following sections were generated from such a witness in which all values were shifted such that the first arrival time is at time 0.

div.head: C. Constraints for N subsystems
div.p: The above constraints have to be adapted for systems with more than two subsystems. The difficulty is in the reason that a job may be delayed, i.e., in the definition of s n ia n i . For two subsystems, if a job is deferred, then this must have been delayed or blocked by a job of the other subsystem. It cannot have been deferred by a job from the same subsystem, because overrun that falls into the next budget period is subtracted from the budget of the next job. The deferral of a job can therefore be characterized using the rather simple formulae of constraints 1 and 2.

For more than two processes, we need to replace those first two constraints by more elaborate ones. We observe that the total deferral of a job i, n can be seen to consist of two parts, which we will call d1 n i and d2 n i :
div.formula: s n i -a n i = d1 n i + d2 n i
div.p: The first part, d1 n i , is the amount of time that i, n has to wait until currently running jobs allow it to start: if, at the time of arrival, higher priority jobs were running, then these must finish first; if only lower priority jobs were running, then they need to free any shared resources first. An example is given in Figure 2.
Suppose l, k is the highest priority job that is running when i, n arrives:
div.formula: R n i = { j, m | s m j ≤ a n i < f m j } l, k = arg min j,m ∈R n i (j)
div.p: Then we can define bounds on d1 n i based on the l. If l, k was of a lower priority, then i, n will start competing with other jobs after l, k frees any shared resources. This can defer i, n at most X l time units. If l, k was of the same subsystem as i, n , then the new job needs to wait until the old one ends. It can also be the case that l, k has a higher priority than i, n . In that case, we define H n i as the set of jobs from R n i that have a higher priority than i, n . Job i, n must wait until all of these have finished, before it can compete

div.p: with jobs that have not yet started.
div.formula: H n i = { j, m | j, m ∈ R n i ∧ j < i}      0 ≤ d1 n i < min(X l , f k l -a n i ) i < l d1 n i = Q i -q n i i = l d1 n i = max j,m ∈H n i f m j -a n i i > l
div.p: Now we have bounds on d1 n i , we can define the additional delay that i, n may suffer, due to higher priority jobs that might have arrived. The job will have to wait until no other jobs of a higher priority subsystem need to run. This extra deferral can be defined much like the waiting time:
div.formula: D n i = { j, m | a n i + d1 n i ≤ s m j < s n i ∧ j < i} d2 n i = j,m ∈D n i e m j -w m j
div.p: The system of constraints that we have now obtained characterizes failure traces for systems consisting of more than one subsystem. However, most of the results in the remainder of this paper have been generated with the 2-subsystem version of the SMT version, as it generates formulae that are much quicker to solve. All depicted failure traces can be reproduced with the N -process solver, though, and generation of a number of additional counterexamples has given us confidence in the correctness of both models.

div.head: V. RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we first reflect on the findings in [11], [12], and verify that the results presented there can be reproduced with our analysis.

Although we originally set out to find an exact schedulability test for the general problem with more than two processes, it seems that even for two processes it is not straightforward to devise such a test. The results discussed in Sections V-B-V-D imply that the regular approach of doing worst-case response time analysis will not work in our case.

div.head: A. Schedulability gain
div.p: An exact schedulability analysis for FPPS with overrun and without payback is interesting if it allows for better schedulability of subsystems. In [11], [12], it was noted that out of the example systems from that paper, all could be scheduled with HS-rbo, while a substantial amount of systems could not be scheduled using HS-o. Using our SMT analysis, we have checked this result.

Although our SMT strategy only allows us to decide for a concrete choice of task set whether it is schedulable, it is reasonable to assume that the problem is monotonic in the sense that an increase of Q 1 or X 1 will never make an unschedulable system schedulable. This assumption implies that a minimal value for Q 1 given X 1 (resp. X 1 given Q 1 ) for which the system is still schedulable can be found doing a simple binary search. We collected these minimal values for a number of different values for Q 1 and X 1 . The results are shown in Figure 3.
Fig. 3. The example system from [11], [12], and the schedulable areas using HS-o (left) and HS-rbo (right).
The gain is however not always so dramatic. In fact, the schedulable area is the same for both forms of scheduling for the system depicted in Figure 6.

div.head: B. Critical instant
div.p: Usually, RTA assumes some critical instant, as was introduced in [18]; a starting state from which a deadline will be missed if the system is unschedulable. Existing analysis assumes that a critical instant for the lowest priority subsystem is the situation in which that subsystem and all higher priority subsystems start simultaneously [7], [11], [12]. The assumption is that the system exhibits worst-case behaviour at the critical instant, in which case it is sufficient to see if the system is schedulable at the critical instant. We have identified systems for the two-subsystem problem that are unschedulable because of a deadline miss of the lowest priority subsystem, but that are schedulable when both subsystems are released simultaneously. Fig. 4.

A system that is schedulable if the subsystems are released simultaneously. At the top, a scenario with simultaneous release and maximal overrun. At the bottom, an illustration of its unschedulability in the general case (with ε = 0.01). The deadline miss is marked by .

One such system is depicted in figure 4. It is easy to see why no deadlines are missed when the subsystems are released simultaneously. Subsystem S 0 cannot miss a deadline because X 1 is simply too small. Because P 1 = 2P 0 , a simultaneous release guarantees that no more than two instances of subsystem S 0 occur in a period of subsystem S 1 . This is not enough to make subsystem S 1 miss a deadline, because

It is interesting to compare this example with HS-o. While the failure trace is also valid for HS-o, the analysis for that form of scheduling assumes simultaneous release to be a critical instant for S 1 . Indeed, when using HS-o, a simultaneous release causes job 1, 0 to be allowed an overrun that extends 1 + ε time units into the next budget period. As this amount is not being paid back (where it is paid back when using HS-rbo), the interference for the next job is 2 • 0.5 + 1 + ε, causing the next job to finish 0.5 + ε after its deadline.

In Figure 4, an example trace is shown in which both subsystems are released simultaneously and scheduled using HS-rbo. It is clear that no deadline can be missed, because the amount of interference from S 0 is constant in every period of S 1 , and any overrun of S 1 is treated as computation time for the next job.

div.head: C. Maximal overrun
div.p: Another aspect that makes regular RTA difficult, is the fact that in some cases it is necessary for subsystem S 1 to have less than maximal overrun in order to miss its deadline later. An example of such a system is shown in figure 5. Note that in this figure, the second and sixth job of S 0 are delayed a little bit, although this is not visible from the figure itself. It is easy to see that in this figure, an increase of the overrun time of the third job of subsystem S 1 would break the counterexample: the starting delay of the second and third job of subsystem S 1 would be increased with the same amount. However, if the third job starts later, then it must also claim its resource later, or otherwise its overrun would not be maximal. But it cannot claim its resource later, because subsystem S 0 would then be able to preempt it.

Indeed adding to our SMT specification the assumption that v n i > Y , for large enough Y , causes the formula to be unsatisfiable. Theorem 1, presented later in this paper, gives rise to a simple proof that demanding maximal overrun indeed makes the system schedulable.

div.head: D. Arbitrary length failure traces
div.p: A consequence of not having a fixed critical instant is that there is no reason to assume the existence of an upper bound for the size of a failure trace. Usually, it is assumed that it suffices to look at a bounded time interval, as was done in [19]. However, if we take a system as described in figure 6, we obtain increasingly long failure traces as we decrease Q 1 towards 1.5 whilst leaving X 1 at a constant value.
Fig. 6. System with arbitrary length counterexamples. On top, a failure trace having Q 1 = 1.8 and X 1 = 0.5. Below that, one with Q 1 = 1.7 and X 1 = 0.5. The deadline miss is marked by .

We mentioned before that our SMT analysis only tries to find counterexamples of bounded length. In Figure 7, the '+' marks show the estimation of the feasible area, when looking for counterexamples with 10 or less instances of subsystem S 0 . The estimation is rather inaccurate: the real feasible area is bounded by the line 2 -Q 1 . Q1 X1 Fig. 7. The schedulable area is bounded by X 1 ≤ 1 and Q 1 + X 1 ≤ P 1 -P 1 P 0 Q 0 . The two solid dots indicate the failure traces from Figure 6.
The explanation is that this type of counterexample, in which the n-th instance of subsystem S 1 misses its deadline, can be characterized by the following inequality:
div.formula: nQ 1 + (n -1)X 1 ≤ nP 1 - nP 1 P 0 Q 0
div.p: The left hand side of this equation expresses the upper bound on the time needed to execute n jobs of subsystem S 1 , n -1 of which have maximal overrun. The right hand side is the amount of time available to do this amount of work in: n times the budget period of subsystem S 1 , minus the time that is taken by subsystem S 0 during that period.

In Figure 7 we have plotted this inequality as light gray lines for 1 ≤ n ≤ 50. As n approaches infinity, the inequality approaches Q 1 + X 1 ≤ P 1 -P1 P0 Q 0 , which corresponds to the solid line 2 -Q 1 . As an infinitely long failure trace is not a failure trace (they are finite by definition), scenarios with sufficiently small values of X 1 that fall on this line are still schedulable. The line 2 -Q 1 therefore bounds the true schedulable area in Figure 7.

div.head: VI. EXACT ANALYSIS FOR TWO SUBSYSTEMS
div.p: As an initial step towards a schedulability analysis for the general problem, we give an analysis for the problem restricted to two subsystems. Testing whether S 0 can miss a deadline is trivial, as this is possible if and only if X 1 > P 0 -Q 0 . We therefore focus on finding a formula that is true if and only if S 1 can miss a deadline.

We propose for the 2-subsystem problem an alternative for using a notion of critical instant. Instead, we use the following theorem, which says that if there is a failure trace, then the end of that trace looks like Figure 8a.

Theorem 1: If subsystem S 1 can miss its deadline, then a failure trace exists in which a k 0 = s k 0 = a n+1 1 -Q 0 , where 1, n is the job that misses its deadline, and 0, k is the last job blocking 1, n .

Proof: Note that a deadline miss of subsystem S 1 is always a result of too many executions of subsystem S 0 occurring in a single period of subsystem S 1 . The minimum number of executions of subsystem S 0 in a single period of subsystem S 1 is M = P1 P0 . Because periods are equal to deadlines, a job from subsystem S 1 can never be preempted or deferred by more than M + 2 jobs from subsystem S 0 . We distinguish three cases:

div.p: The analysis for two subsystems hints at a possible approach to develop a general analysis that also allows simultaneous access of multiple resources: the current analysis can be seen as a reachability analysis. Model checking techniques might therefore allow us to specify the scheduling problem in a more intuitive way than by manually creating an SMT model. A schedulability analysis could then directly be given as a parameterised boolean equation system, a formalism that can directly capture the equation given in section VI. It is likely that quite some extra work would be needed to simplify the generated results, but the approach seems less troublesome than the manual approach we followed in this paper.

Subsystem S 1 could have been deferred by subsystem S 0 for long enough, but only if the deferring job itself was again deferred by subsystem S 1 . This can only happen if the job of subsystem S 0 was deferred for less than X 1 time units. If the previous job of subsystem S 1 indeed deferred subsystem S 0 and ran for less than Q 1 + X 1 time, then a trace leading up to that situation can be extended into a failure trace. If none of the above cases hold, then either subsystem S 0 cannot be deferred for long enough to be able to defer subsystem S 1 for long enough (∆ ≤ P 0 -Q 0 -X 1 , in Figure 8(d) this would amount to x being too small), or the computation time of subsystem S 0 is simply too small to cause the needed delay (∆ ≤ A -Q 0 ).

One special case arises when this equation has both true and false as a solution; in that case, the function apparently recurses infinitely. We may conclude that in this case there is no finite failure trace, hence letting f be the least fixpoint of the equation is justified.

The proposed schedulability analysis was tested on a number of instances, for which it yields the same result as our SMT analysis when the search depth is limited. The complexity of this test is linear in the size of the failure trace. As failure traces are finite per definition, and when all inputs are fractional (as is the case in most practical situations), the check terminates and an upper bound on the computation time can be given quite easily.

For N processes, it is difficult to predict whether this technique will lead to a practical schedulability test. The (c) and (d) cases must then be extended to decide which process was deferring or preempting a job. This leads to a check of complexity O(N l ), where l is the length of the failure trace. Another complication is the fixpoint: infinite recursion must be prevented in order to always terminate. For fractional inputs, this amounts to checking for previously encountered states, but this can still be a rather costly affair when traces grow longer.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have investigated the schedulability of a hierarchical scheduling framework with replenishment-bounded overrun and without payback, HS-rbo in short. An analysis for two subsystems was given using satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), which yielded a number of results that show that the schedulability analysis for FPPS with overrun and payback from [7], [12] cannot be easily extended to deal with this type of scheduling.

In particular, the definition of a critical instant for HS-o is not correct for HS-rbo, failure traces can grow to arbitrary length and maximal blocking does not always lead to a maximal response time.

For more than two subsystems, the SMT model was extended. The resulting model also assumes that global resource access is non-preemptive. Although this is quite a severe restriction for global logical resource sharing in general, it is appropriate for those systems where fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS) is used for local scheduling to reduce the architecture-related preemption costs and to improve feasibility.
